result: Audited Flowise server routes/controllers/services. Found a supported unauthenticated credential-abuse vulnerability: POST /api/v1/text-to-speech/generate is in WHITELIST_URLS (no auth), and when chatflowId is omitted the controller takes provider/credentialId directly from the request body and passes it to convertTextToSpeechStream -> getCredentialData, which looks up the Credential by id only with no workspace/org scoping. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore invoke any stored credential (e.g. OpenAI/ElevenLabs API keys) to generate speech. Other reviewed surfaces (get-upload-file, fetch-links SSRF deny-list, storage path sanitization, vm2 sandbox, MCP token constant-time compare, webhook signature verification, callback dispatcher) were found hardened.

Audited server-side services/utils and node execution paths. Most areas are well-hardened (httpSecurity SSRF deny-list with pinned agents, path traversal guards in validator.ts/BaseStorageProvider, constant-time MCP token compare, HMAC webhook signature verification, stripProtectedFields mass-assignment guard). One supported finding: the whitelisted (unauthenticated) OAuth2 callback GET /api/v1/oauth2-credential/callback resolves the target credential by the attacker-supplied `state` query parameter alone with no workspace/tenant scoping, then overwrites that credential's encryptedData with token data returned from the credential's token endpoint — a cross-tenant credential overwrite/authorization flaw.

Audited enterprise auth/RBAC layer. Found two attacker-reachable authorization gaps: (1) WorkspaceUserController.create/update/delete (POST/PUT/DELETE /api/v1/workspaceuser) lack the getLoggedInUser + assertWorkspaceIdAccessibleToUser/assertQueryOrganizationMatchesActiveOrg tenant guards that the sibling read handler and other enterprise controllers use, allowing a user with workspace:add-user/workspace:unlink-user in one org to add/modify/remove members of a workspace in another org (cross-tenant privilege escalation). (2) POST /api/v1/user (user.route.ts) has no permission check and no tenant guard, and UserController.create passes raw req.body to UserService.createUser, allowing any authenticated principal (including a low-privilege API key) to create arbitrary user accounts, unlike the guarded /account/invite path.

Audited the background-task/queue/schedule runtime and webhook paths. Two supported findings: (1) verifyWebhookSignature derives the HMAC algorithm from the attacker-supplied signature header prefix ('sha1=' downgrade) instead of the flow-configured webhookSignatureType, weakening the sole auth guard on the unauthenticated POST /api/v1/webhook/:id endpoint (services/webhook/index.ts + utils/signatureVerification.ts). (2) webhook-listener unregisterListener omits the assertChatflowIsWebhookTriggered workspace/webhook-trigger check that registerListener and streamListener enforce, allowing a flow-edit user to delete listener registrations for arbitrary chatflow ids (controllers/webhook-listener/index.ts + services/webhook-listener/registry.ts). ScheduleQueue/ScheduleExecutor/ScheduleBeat and callbackDispatcher (secureAxiosRequest) were reviewed and showed no additional attacker-reachable flaw within scope.

Audited Flowise server routes/controllers for auth bypass and IDOR. Confirmed finding: GET /api/v1/feedback/:id (getAllChatMessageFeedback) is in WHITELIST_URLS, so the global auth middleware in packages/server/src/index.ts skips authentication for it. The controller passes the attacker-supplied chatflowId straight to utilGetChatMessageFeedback, which queries ChatMessageFeedback by chatflowid with no ownership/workspace check, returning chatId, messageId, rating and free-text content for any chatflow. chatflowId is publicly discoverable via the also-whitelisted /api/v1/public-chatbotConfig/:id. Other whitelisted routes checked (leads GET requires req.user workspaceId; get-upload-file validates UUID + isUnsafeFilePath and derives orgId; attachments validates UUID/path traversal and file types; public-executions requires isPublic=true; oauth2 callback requires valid code) were adequately guarded.

Audited packages/components/src security helpers and storage providers (httpSecurity.ts, headerValidation.ts, recordManagerSecurity.ts, sanitizeDataSourceOptions.ts, validator.ts, storage/*) plus related server-side attacker-reachable paths (get-upload-file, files, attachments, webhook, mcp-endpoint/mcp-server, callbackDispatcher, executeCustomNodeFunction, apiKey/validateKey, oauth2Security, signatureVerification, sanitizeFlowData, stripProtectedFields). All reviewed sinks are guarded: SSRF via secureAxiosRequest/secureFetch with DNS-pinned agents and deny-list; path traversal via sanitizeFilename/isUnsafeFilePath/validateChatflowId in BaseStorageProvider.buildPath; header injection via validateCustomHeaders; SQL identifier injection via sanitizeRecordManagerTableName; TypeORM RCE via sanitizeDataSourceOptions; webhook auth via constant-time HMAC/plain-token verification; MCP token via timingSafeEqual; API keys via scrypt+timingSafeEqual; vm2 sandbox forces require/eval/wasm off. No supported exploitable vulnerability identified within scope.

Audited server utils/services file-handling and validation helpers. Most are well-guarded (get-upload-file uses isValidUUID+isUnsafeFilePath; createAttachment validates MIME/extension and path traversal; sanitizeFlowData strips credentials; signatureVerification uses timingSafeEqual; oauth2Security enforces domain allowlist + HTTPS by default). Found one supported authorization flaw: the OAuth2 credential routes (packages/server/src/routes/oauth2/index.ts) mount /refresh/:credentialId and /callback with NO auth middleware, and both are in WHITELIST_URLS (utils/constants.ts) so they are reachable unauthenticated. Unlike /authorize/:credentialId (which scopes the credential lookup by getActiveWorkspaceIdForRequest), /refresh and /callback look up the Credential by id/state alone with no workspace scoping, enabling cross-workspace credential access (IDOR) and unauthenticated token refresh/leak of token metadata.

Audited webhook/schedule/mcp-endpoint/mcp-server services. Confirmed: (1) webhook route is unauthenticated at route level (routes/webhook/index.ts) and downstream auth via validateFlowAPIKey returns true when chatflow.apikeyid is null, while webhookEnableAuth defaults to false — webhook-triggered flows are publicly invocable without credentials. (2) MCP endpoint token verification and mcp-server config routes are properly authorized (constant-time compare, RBAC). (3) callbackUrl SSRF is mitigated by secureAxiosRequest deny-list. (4) Schedule execution is internal-only and RBAC-gated. Primary finding: unauthenticated webhook invocation / auth bypass.

Audited Flowise server routes/controllers. Confirmed an unauthenticated cross-tenant information disclosure: GET /api/v1/feedback/:id (whitelisted, no auth) reaches feedbackController.getAllChatMessageFeedback -> feedbackService.getAllChatMessageFeedback -> utilGetChatMessageFeedback, which queries ChatMessageFeedback by chatflowid only with no workspace/ownership check, returning all feedback (content, chatId) for any chatflow UUID. Also noted the webhook-listener streamListener registers an SSE client under an attacker-supplied listenerId without validating it against the registry.

Audited packages/components security utilities and node execution paths. Most modules are hardened: httpSecurity.ts (SSRF deny-list + pinned agents + redirect validation), headerValidation.ts (CRLF/hop-by-hop/sensitive header rejection), recordManagerSecurity.ts, sanitizeDataSourceOptions.ts, validator.ts (path traversal/MIME), MCP core.ts (command allowlist + flag/injection/env validation), and the vm2/E2B code sandbox. One guard-coverage gap identified: LocalStorageProvider.getFileFromUpload() and removeSpecificFileFromUpload() perform fs.readFileSync/fs.unlinkSync on a raw, unsanitized path, unlike every sibling method which routes through sanitizeFilename()/buildPath()/validatePathSecurity(). Reported as a finding.

Audited dynamic-execution and MCP paths. Findings: (1) POST /api/v1/node-load-method/:name (routes/node-load-methods/index.ts) has NO permission check, unlike the sibling node-custom-functions route which requires chatflows:create/update. It reaches nodesService.getSingleNodeAsyncOptions which invokes nodeInstance.loadMethods[attacker-controlled methodName].call(nodeInstance, attacker-controlled nodeData, ...) — an authorization gap letting any authenticated principal (incl. low-privilege API keys) invoke arbitrary node load methods. (2) MCP endpoint auth (constant-time token compare), custom-mcp-servers SSRF guard (checkDenyList + isValidURL), webhook callbackUrl (secureAxiosRequest), get-upload-file/attachments path guards (isUnsafeFilePath/isValidUUID/sanitizeFilename) were reviewed and found adequately guarded. (3) executeCustomNodeFunction runs user JS via NodeVM with child_process/fs/process undefined and builtin deps excluding them — guarded.

Audited file upload/download paths. get-upload-file, attachments, and storage providers (Local/S3/GCS/Azure) all validate chatflowId as UUID, sanitize filenames, and block path traversal; /files route is commented out (unreachable). Found a cross-tenant credential abuse issue: routes/openai-assistants-files/index.ts mounts POST /upload/ with no checkPermission guard, and services/openai-assistants/index.ts looks up the credential by id only (findOneBy({id: credentialId})) with no workspace scoping, so any authenticated principal can use another workspace's OpenAI credential. Also getFileFromAssistant (public/whitelisted) lacks controller-level validation but is mitigated by provider guards.
